result.summary: Under King Phintas the Messenians send a choir to Delos, and the first quarrel with Sparta arises at a temple of Artemis Limnas, with two rival accounts. A generation later, the wrong done to the Messenian Polychares by the Spartan Euæphnus leads to open strife.

scenes.title: Messenian offering to Delos
scenes.summary: In Phintas' reign the Messenians first send sacrifices and a men's choir to Apollo at Delos, with a hymn by Eumelus.

scenes.title: Quarrel at Artemis Limnas
scenes.summary: Sparta and Messenia give conflicting accounts of how King Teleclus died at the temple on their border.
scenes.stakes: Teleclus is killed; the maidens' honour (Spartan version) or Spartan treachery exposed (Messenian version).

scenes.title: Strife begins under new kings
scenes.summary: A generation later, Sparta begins hostilities on a plausible pretext, which could have been settled by arbitration.

scenes.title: Polychares wronged by Euæphnus
scenes.summary: Euæphnus sells Polychares' cattle, then kills his son; denied justice by Sparta, Polychares goes mad with rage and kills Spartans.
scenes.stakes: Polychares loses his property and his son, and his sanity.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses both names for the people of Sparta.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias openly leaves readers to choose between rival accounts.
Euæphnus' plea that love of gain compels injustice.

analysis.text: The passage shows how wars arise from disputed wrongs, with each side telling a self-justifying story.
It prepares the account of the First Messenian War, which Sparta used to subjugate Messenia, and Pausanias weighs local traditions.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says the hymn to Delos was the only genuine work of Eumelus, showing ancient doubts about attributions.

language_notes.text: Processional hymn (prosodion) was sung by a choir as it approached the altar; the Messenian offering to Delos was of this kind.
"Persons of quality" means Messenian nobles; "beardless" means youths too young to grow beards, so they could pass as girls.
"Specious" means seeming right or fair but not truly so; the pretext looked reasonable but was misleading.
Games were dated by Olympiads, four-year cycles; the fourth Olympiad falls about 758 BC. Only the footrace was then contested.
Ephors were the five annually elected Spartan magistrates who held great power alongside the two kings.

context_notes.text: Eumelus was an early Corinthian poet; Pausanias doubts that much work ascribed to him is genuine.
Artemis Limnas, "of the marsh," had a shared sanctuary on the Laconian-Messenian frontier. Dorians were one of the main Greek peoples.
Sparta had two royal houses ruling at once; here Alcamenes and Theopompus, one from each family.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias steps back as a historian, presenting both accounts and leaving judgment to the reader instead of settling the dispute.
Euæphnus is shown as greedy and smooth-tongued through his deceit, making his later betrayal of a friend unsurprising.
Polychares seeks justice from Spartan authorities and is refused, so he turns to indiscriminate violence himself.
